notes.story: Publications desk item 18: recalibrated argon-argon dating on eight sanidine samples from Oplontis gives 1,938 +/- 13 years against 1,946 years from Pliny the Younger's account (Berkeley Geochronology Center, UC Berkeley, University of Padua; Paul Renne).
caveats_on_screen: Slide 2: the eyewitness is Pliny the Younger, who was 17 at the time and wrote his account as an adult; 'a Roman teenager's letter' is not used.
Slide 3: the samples are from Oplontis, not Pompeii itself.
Slide 6: the exact day of the eruption is debated; it is not put on screen. The year is given as AD 79. The day debate shifts the benchmark by weeks, negligible against +/- 13 years.
Compare slide: the 'myth' is a common assumption, not a quote from anyone.
notes.fact_check: 2026-09-27 wave 2 GREEN (hook AMBER): Science Advances, 25 Sept 2026. Berkeley Geochronology Center, UC Berkeley, University of Padua; Paul Renne leads. Eight sanidine samples from pumice at Oplontis; 1,938 +/- 13 years before the 2025 analysis vs 1,946 years from Pliny the Younger's account; precision 0.7%, accuracy 0.4%; potassium-40 half-life 12.044 +/- 0.088 billion years, twice as precise as before. Say 'an eyewitness account by Pliny the Younger, who was 17 at the time'; say 'AD 79', not a day. Required wording applied.

caption:
Eight sanidine samples from the AD 79 Vesuvius eruption, collected at Oplontis, were dated with a recalibrated argon-argon method: 1,938 plus or minus 13 years, against 1,946 years from Pliny the Younger's eyewitness account. Precision 0.7%, accuracy 0.4%. The exact day of the eruption is debated; the year is not. Paul Renne, Berkeley Geochronology Center, UC Berkeley, University of Padua. Science Advances, 25 September 2026. Which ancient event would you calibrate against?

slides.title: The eruption that buried Pompeii just *recalibrated* Earth's clock
slides.sub: Argon-argon dating tested against a date we already know: AD 79. Science Advances, September 2026.

slides.title: A date we already *know*
slides.body: Pliny the Younger, 17 at the time, left an eyewitness account of the AD 79 eruption. That fixes its age at 1,946 years and gives geologists a benchmark to test their method against.

slides.title: *Sanidine* from the eruption's pumice
slides.body: Eight samples, collected at Oplontis rather than Pompeii itself, dated with the argon-argon method.

slides.title: years, by recalibrated argon-argon dating
slides.body: The known age is 1,946 years. The measurement lands within its own error bar: precision 0.7%, accuracy 0.4%.

slides.myth: A radiometric date is either exactly right or wrong
slides.body: A known date lets the method be checked and its calibration tightened. The potassium-40 half-life is now 12.044 ± 0.088 billion years, twice as precise as before.

slides.title: The exact *day* is debated
slides.body: Scholars disagree about which day in AD 79 Vesuvius erupted. A shift of weeks is negligible against a 13-year error bar, so the benchmark holds.

slides.title: Paul Renne, *Berkeley Geochronology Center*
slides.body: With UC Berkeley and the University of Padua. Science Advances, 25 September 2026.
